lines.text: Kingdoms that faced Portugal, a queen who fought back, centuries of the slave trade, then a long war for freedom and peace. This is the story of Angola.
Around 1390, in the north of today's Angola, a city rose that would be the capital of a great kingdom: Mbanza Kongo.
The Kingdom of Kongo spread across west-central Africa. When the Portuguese arrived in the 1480s, its kings took up Christianity.
King Afonso the First made Kongo Christian, and wrote to the king of Portugal against the slave trade draining his people.
Further south, in the highlands, the Mbundu people had their own kingdom, Ndongo.
In 1576 the Portuguese founded Luanda on the coast. It is now Angola's capital.
Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba bargained with the Portuguese, and fought them, and kept her people free for decades.
But Portugal held on. Its colony became a great source of enslaved people shipped to Brazil.
In 1922 Agostinho Neto was born. A poet, he would become the first president of a free Angola.
Jonas Savimbi, born in 1934, would lead the rebel movement UNITA through decades of war.
Jose Eduardo dos Santos, born in 1942, would rule as president for thirty-eight years.
The roots of Sonangol, the state oil company, go back to 1953. Oil would come to dominate the country's wealth.
Joao Lourenco, born in 1954, would succeed dos Santos as president in 2017.
In 1956 the MPLA was founded, the movement that has ruled Angola since independence.
In 1961 the war against Portuguese rule began, and it went on for thirteen years.
In 1966 Savimbi founded UNITA, a rival movement that would later fight the MPLA.
In January 1975, at Alvor, a deal set independence for November. It soon collapsed into war.
Cuba sent tens of thousands of troops to fight for the MPLA, and they stayed until 1991.
Independence came in November 1975, and with it a civil war that would last more than a quarter of a century.
Even in wartime, Angolans made something new: kizomba, a slow, close dance and music now loved around the world.
In 1987 Angolan and Cuban forces fought South Africa at Cuito Cuanavale, one of the largest battles of the war.
In 1992 the republic took its present form. Ten years later, after Savimbi's death, peace at last came to Angola.
From the kingdom of Kongo to a land at peace, Angola's long story goes on.
